justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a modestly bullish near-term outlook anchored around recent price levels, with a gentle upward drift over longer horizons. For the 1-day estimate of 278.5, I was largely extrapolating from the prevailing market price with minimal expected movement, since single-day price changes in most liquid assets or indices tend to be small relative to their level. The 1-week estimate of 280.0 incorporates a slight positive drift, consistent with the historical tendency of equity markets or similar instruments to trend upward over short periods when no major catalysts are expected. The 1-month estimate of 283.0 extends that drift further, reflecting a rough annualized return assumption in the low-to-mid single digits, discounted to a monthly increment.

The confidence interval widths widen substantially as the time horizon extends, which reflects the well-established statistical property that uncertainty compounds over time. For the 1-day interval of roughly ±8.5 points, I was drawing on typical daily volatility estimates — perhaps 1–2% for a moderately volatile instrument. The 1-week interval of ±17 points and the 1-month interval of ±33 points scale approximately with the square root of time, consistent with a random walk or geometric Brownian motion framework. The asymmetry is kept relatively modest because I did not have strong reason to believe the distribution was heavily skewed in either direction at the time of the forecast.

Specific risks that could push outcomes outside the stated intervals include sudden macroeconomic shocks such as an unexpected central bank policy announcement, a geopolitical escalation, or a surprise inflation or employment print. On the upside, better-than-expected earnings results, a dovish pivot signal, or a resolution of an ongoing trade or geopolitical tension could push prices above the upper bound. Tail events — financial contagion, a major institutional failure, or a sudden liquidity crisis — represent the most serious downside risks capable of breaching the lower bound of the 1-month interval.

It is also worth noting that my intervals, being 90% confidence bands, are explicitly designed to be violated roughly 10% of the time under the assumed model. The real world frequently produces distributions with fatter tails than standard models assume, meaning the true probability of an extreme outcome is likely somewhat higher than the 5% I allocated to each tail. Structural breaks, regime changes, or correlated shocks across markets are the kinds of events most likely to cause my stated intervals to prove too narrow.
